title: Deploy requirements
description: What a deployment needs from GitHub, by name: deploy/requirements.json for the shared repository variables, and deploy/<provider>/requirements.json for a provider's environments, variables and secrets. The deploy preflight (.github/actions/deploy-preflight) checks them before any cloud step. Names and rules only, never a value.

guide.description: The guide that explains these settings, from the repository root, such as docs/deploy/upcloud.md. Each `step` is a link into it.

environments.description: The provider's GitHub environments, by name. Each must exist and be limited to the `main` branch. Only a provider's file has them.

name.description: A variable or secret name as GitHub allows it, in capitals. Names starting with GITHUB_ or PREFLIGHT_ are taken.

step.description: The guide step that fixes it, as a link into the guide, such as #4-create-the-environments-in-your-fork.

reviewers.description: "required": the environment must have required reviewers, so each run waits for an approval (the deploy environment). "none": it must have none, so a scheduled run never waits (the cleanup environment).

variables.description: The environment's own variables, by name, read by the jobs that use it.

secrets.description: The environment's secrets, by name. The workflow passes each one to the preflight step through `env:`, under its own name.

required.description: Whether it must be set. Default false: optional, but checked when set.

pattern.description: A regular expression (JavaScript syntax) the whole value must match. Anchor it with ^ and $.

minimum.description: The smallest number allowed. The value must then be a number.

maximum.description: The largest number allowed. The value must then be a number.

example.description: An allowed value, shown when the value is wrong.

environments.description: The environments whose jobs read it. Default: all of the provider's environments, and every job for a shared variable.

secret.description: Only checked for being set and matching its pattern. Its value, or any part of it, is never printed. A secret has no example, so nothing that looks like a real one is ever written down.
